title: An Instance's Network field names where the position sits, not where its controls live
content:
A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.3.6.1.1.2.1.1 declares the Instance's Network as **Monad**, and the Atlas files it under "A.6.1.1.2.2.6.1.3.6 - Monad Instances." Its Contract Addresses section then lists a Pool Address and USDC address on Monad — and a third entry at .2.2.3: "**Broker Address (Ethereum Mainnet)** `0xD94F9ef3…`".

The rate limits are metered at that broker leg, not at the pool. So a single Instance spans two chains: the exposure is on Monad, the enforcement is on Ethereum.

This makes the Network field an attribute of the *destination* rather than of the Instance as a whole, and the Atlas's per-network organisation inherits that meaning. Enumerating "Ethereum Mainnet Instances" therefore understates what is actually being controlled from Ethereum, and enumerating "Monad Instances" overstates what is controlled on Monad.

The practical consequence is for anyone reasoning about chain-level risk. A question like "what happens if chain X halts?" cannot be answered from the Instance groupings, because an Instance's liveness may depend on a chain other than the one it is filed under. Here, a Monad position's ability to receive capital depends on Ethereum, and its ability to return capital depends on FalconX — neither of which is visible from the heading.

The schema has room to make this legible: it already distinguishes address entries by network in the label. What it lacks is any field that records the *control path* as distinct from the position, so the information survives only as a parenthetical in an address name.
description: The Monad Uniswap Instance declares Network: Monad while listing a Broker Address on Ethereum Mainnet and metering its rate limit there, so grouping Instances by chain misstates each chain's
